_work.title: [Treatise on Charms and Talismans] (Princeton, Third Series no. 591, 1483 CE)
_work.blurb: A 26-leaf Arabic manuscript treatise on charms and talismans (amulets), dated 1483 CE, held at Princeton University Library (Third Series no. 591). The MS contains multiple types of Islamic magical diagrams: pentagonal khatim talisman seals (pentagon star circles with Arabic numerals), red-bordered wafq letter grids, triangular staircase letter-combination tables (muhmal arrangements), and full-page diamond-lattice letter grids — all typical of the late medieval Arabic huruf/talisman tradition. The diamond-lattice grid (a diagonal crossing of letter-rows, producing a net of rhombus cells each containing an Arabic letter or combination) is a distinctive Islamic visual formula for encoding divine-name letter combinations in a spatially memorable way. The manuscript was compiled in 1483 CE, placing it in the same generation as the earliest European printed books and the high point of Ottoman imperial expansion — a period when Islamic talismanic manuscripts circulated widely across the Mediterranean and Middle East.
_work.rights: Public Domain — 1483 CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
_work.creator: Anonymous

entries.title: Pentagon Khatim + Wafq Table + Magical Script Row (Charms MS, p. 22)
entries.summary: A densely diagrammatic page from a 1483 CE Princeton charms-and-talismans MS containing three distinct diagram elements: (1) A 4×5 red-bordered wafq letter grid in the upper section, with Arabic letters in each cell encoding a letter combination sequence; (2) A pentagonal khatim talisman — a pentagon with an internal star and outer circular border, containing Arabic numerals and text at the star points and outer ring — a rare pentagonal talisman form (most Islamic khatims use circles, hexagrams, or squares, making the five-pointed/pentagon configuration unusual and particularly associated with Solomonic magic); (3) A row of Arabic letters/characters in a variant or magical script style at the bottom. The combination of letter-grid, five-pointed-star talisman, and script-row on a single page represents the multi-modal approach of Islamic talismanic manuscripts: the wafq provides the combinatorial letter encoding, the khatim provides the geometric figure to be reproduced, and the script row provides the operative formula to be written or spoken. The pentagonal khatim shape connects to the Solomonic pentagram tradition transmitted through the Arabic Picatrix and related grimoire literature.

entries.title: Triangular Staircase Letter Table (Muhmal Arrangement) — Charms MS (p. 23)
entries.summary: A page from the 1483 CE Princeton charms MS showing a triangular staircase letter-combination arrangement — a pattern where rows of Arabic letters descend in a stair-step progression, each row offset from the previous to create a visual diagonal cascade. This muhmal (mute/unpointed letter) staircase arrangement is a classic huruf/letter-science diagram used to display all possible letter combinations in a systematic visual form, beginning with single letters at the top and expanding to multi-letter sequences below. The arrangement serves both as a mnemonic device (the visual pattern aids memorization of letter sequences) and as an operative talisman template (the staircase form itself is geometrically meaningful in the tradition). A smaller red-bordered bordered table appears above the staircase section. This type of descending-staircase letter arrangement is found across Islamic manuscripts from al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif through Ottoman talismanic compilations, representing the interface between combinatorial mathematics and mystical letter science.

entries.title: Full-Page Diamond-Lattice Letter Grid — Charms MS (p. 37)
entries.summary: A spectacular full-page diamond-lattice letter grid from the 1483 CE Princeton charms MS. The grid is constructed by drawing diagonal lines in two directions (45° and 135°) across the page, creating a network of rhombus-shaped (diamond) cells, each containing an Arabic letter or letter combination. The result is a geometrically striking large-format diagram where the letter content and the geometric form are inseparable — the diamond-net structure is the talismanic form, not merely a container for text. Diamond-lattice letter grids of this type appear in the Shams al-Ma'arif tradition and related Arabic magical manuscripts, where they encode divine names, Quranic verses, or permutations of a specific root across the grid in a way that creates visual as well as numerological coherence. The use of red ink for the diagonal ruling contrasts with the black ink letters, making the lattice itself visually prominent. The grid nearly fills the entire leaf, making this one of the most ambitious single-page talismanic compositions in this compact 26-leaf manuscript.

entries.title: Two Red-Bordered Letter Wafq Tables — Charms MS (p. 40)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
entries.summary: A page from the 1483 CE Princeton charms MS containing two distinct red-bordered wafq letter tables stacked vertically: one in the upper section (approximately 4×5 cells) and another in the lower section (approximately 4×8 cells). Both grids contain Arabic letters in each cell, bordered with red-ink ruling. The double-table format on a single leaf represents an efficient talismanic compilation approach — two distinct charm formulas (keyed to different divine names, Quranic verses, or planetary correspondences) occupying one page. In the Arabic talismanic tradition, letter grids with red-ink borders function both as textual elements and as replicable talisman templates: the practitioner reproduces the exact grid on a suitable medium (paper, metal, cloth) for operative use. The presence of two grids suggests sequential treatment — perhaps two chapters or two applications of the same letter-science system. The red-ink bordering tradition links this Princeton MS directly to the al-Buni / Shams al-Ma'arif tradition of red-accented talismanic manuscripts.
